intro_html: Shogayaki is one of the most ordered lunches in Japan, and it takes about ten minutes to cook. Thin slices of pork get a light dusting of flour, hit a hot pan, and then a ginger sauce of soy, mirin, and sugar goes in and reduces around them into a glaze. The flour is the trick most people skip, and it is what makes the sauce cling to the meat instead of pooling in the pan. Onions cook down in the same sauce and go on top of the rice with everything else.
cost_closing_html: About $2.55 a bowl (at everyday cost) for a Japanese lunch-counter staple with a serious amount of pork in it.
shop_smart: Pork loin is the cheap cut that works here because it is sliced thin. Thin slices cook in seconds and never get the chance to dry out, which is why you do not need to pay up for tenderloin.
Firm the loin in the freezer for half an hour before slicing. That one step lets a regular kitchen knife cut it as thin as the pre-sliced hot pot packs that cost twice as much.
Fresh ginger is the entire identity of this dish. Buy a big knob, grate what you need, and freeze the rest. Powder will not get you there.
Mirin and soy sauce are two bottles that cover a dozen dinners. Once they are in the pantry the recurring cost of this meal is basically the pork and the rice.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Firm the pork loin in the freezer for about thirty minutes, then slice it as thin as you can against the grain.
Grate the ginger and whisk it with the soy sauce, mirin, chicken broth, and sugar to make the ginger sauce.
Toss the pork slices in a light coating of the all-purpose flour and shake off the excess.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat and cook the sliced yellow onions until they soften and start to color, then set them aside.
Cook the pork in batches in a single layer, about a minute per side, until just browned. Crowding the pan is what turns this into a steamed gray mess.
Return all the pork and the onions to the pan, pour in the ginger sauce, and let it bubble until it thickens and coats everything.
Cook the rice according to the package and season the pork with salt and black pepper to taste.
portion_html: Weigh the rice pot and the pork pan separately, subtracting the empty-pot weight from Step 1, and divide each by 14. Even rice underneath, even weight of pork and glazed onion on top, and pour the extra sauce over the containers rather than leaving it in the pan. Every bowl lands near 612 calories with 41 grams of protein.

steps: Firm the pork loin in the freezer and slice it very thin.
Whisk grated ginger with soy sauce, mirin, broth, and sugar.
Dust the pork slices lightly with flour.
Cook the sliced onions until softened, then set aside.
Sear the pork in batches, return the onions, and add the ginger sauce to glaze.
Cook the rice and portion the pork and sauce over it into 14 containers.
